title: Repeat speculations by the same speaker
note: One speculation per speaker per work: when a speaker has speculations in several works, the one with the widest scope of change counts, ties to the earliest. The others are kept here, out of every count and reading. Distinct speculations within one work (scenarios, concept cards, a workshop's statements) all count.

speculations.text: The moving picture art will largely supplement the art of printing.
speculations.speaker: Inventor
speculations.source: Frank Parker Hulette, interview with Thomas Edison, Moving Picture World, 22 July 1911, pp. 104–105. Compiled in “Thomas Edison’s Education Predictions”, muninn.net.

tetrad_detail.enhance: printing, which moving pictures will “largely supplement”

speculations.text: I believe that the motion picture is destined to revolutionize our educational system and that in a few years it will supplant largely, if not entirely, the use of textbooks.
speculations.speaker: Inventor
speculations.source: Hugh Weir, “The Story of the Motion Picture”, McClure’s 54, November 1922, p. 85; quoted in Cuban (1986).
speculations.verify: Full wording taken from secondary sources; check against McClure’s.

tetrad_detail.enhance: the educational system, revolutionised by the motion picture

speculations.text: Textbooks as the principal medium of teaching will be as obsolete as the horse and carriage are now.
speculations.speaker: Inventor
speculations.source: Hugh Weir, “What Edison Would Like to Do with the Movies”, Collier’s 75, 21 February 1925, pp. 20–21. Compiled in muninn.net (as above).

tetrad_detail.obsolesce: textbooks as the principal medium of teaching

speculations.text: I think the computer will blow up the school. … There won’t be schools in the future.
speculations.speaker: Researcher

speculations.text: If you just took the next 18 months, the AIs will come in as a teacher’s aide and give feedback on writing. … The AIs will get to that ability, to be as good a tutor as any human ever could.
speculations.speaker: Company
speculations.source: Bill Gates, ASU+GSV Summit, San Diego, April 2023; reported in CNBC, 22 April 2023.

tetrad_detail.enhance: feedback on writing, and tutoring as good as any human’s

speculations.who: Seymour Papert, interviewed by David S. Bennahum
speculations.text: The power of computers is not to improve school but to replace it with a different kind of structure.
speculations.note: Papert also says future places of learning will “very definitely not” look like schools, and that home computers are “the biggest source of change in education”. He describes school as having absorbed the computer; that is a description of the present, not coded.
speculations.medium_wording: computers, above all in the home
speculations.speaker: Researcher
speculations.source: David S. Bennahum, “School’s Out?”, interview with Seymour Papert, MEME 2.13, 1996 (memex.org); republished on The Daily Papert.
speculations.verify: Original MEME issue and date to confirm; wording via The Daily Papert.

tetrad_detail.obsolesce: school, replaced by “a different kind of structure”

speculations.text: I am convinced that education will undergo the kind of megachange that came in the wake of technological and scientific developments.
speculations.note: Papert reports school’s “immune reaction”: “before the computer could change School, School changed the computer”. This is close to a reversal, but it is reported as what happened, not imagined, so it is not coded. Change is now to come by evolution, not reform.
speculations.speaker: Researcher
speculations.source: Seymour Papert, “Why School Reform Is Impossible”, The Journal of the Learning Sciences 6(4), 1997, pp. 417–427.
speculations.verify: Page of the quoted sentence to confirm against the journal.

speculations.text: Does the computer serve the curriculum or does it make it obsolete? … it makes it also obsolete.
speculations.note: Papert repeats that “school reform is impossible” and that change must “happen in an evolutionary way”.
speculations.speaker: Researcher
speculations.source: Seymour Papert, keynote at SqueakFest, 2006; transcript on The Daily Papert.
